edits.quote: Draw each way in a different copy. (three copies of the hexagon and four copies of the long shape)
edits.fix: The hexagon has exactly 2 blue coverings and the long shape exactly 3, so a K-1 child will treat the empty fourth/third copy as a missing answer and keep hunting or draw a repeat. Either print 2 hexagon copies and 3 long-shape copies, or add 'You may not need every copy.'

edits.quote: For each shape, would you rather go first or second? (with 'first   second' printed under each shape)
edits.fix: Say how to answer: 'For each shape, circle whether you would rather go first or second.'

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 (page number set apart at the right margin)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

k-1.summary: A clean, substantive K-1 sheet: every board is at actual size, the impossible shapes in Problem 1 have even area (so trying them meets the coloring obstruction), the fewest-green triangles (2, 3, 4, 5), the flip puzzles (2 and 4 moves), and the covering game (hexagon: second player wins; strip and trapezoid: first player wins) are all correct. Problem 4 gives more copies than there are coverings, and Problem 6 does not say to circle, so the child can't tell when they are done. Volume is close to forty minutes for a quick child.

edits.quote: Each board below is a big hexagon with two gray holes, and no block may cover a hole. Which of these boards can be covered with blue blocks? For each board that cannot be covered, explain why.
edits.fix: Cut the description the diagram already gives and say how to record: 'No block may cover a gray hole. Cover each board that you can and draw your blocks on it; put an X on each board that cannot be covered and explain why beside it.' (A and D can be covered; B and C cannot.)

edits.quote: Unlabeled boards E and F from Problem 1 sit at the top of page 2, Problem 2 starts below them, and its triangles C and D run onto page 3
edits.fix: Give boards E and F their own page (or keep them with Problem 1) and start Problem 2 on a fresh page, so two problems never share a page while blocks are on it.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 (page number set apart at the right margin)

grades-2-3.summary: This is the strongest band. It is a tightly sequenced development of kernel 1: possible and impossible boards (every impossible board has even area), boards with holes, the fewest-green triangles 2-3-4-5, a proof of the bound for side 4, generalizing to sides 10 and 100, purple chevrons (4, 5, 4, 5 greens, never better than blue), and an invent-a-board task. All of it is correct and all boards are at actual size. Only small recording and page-break fixes are needed.

edits.quote: For the first pair, explain why it cannot be done in fewer moves.
edits.fix: Pair 1 runs between the two extreme coverings (8 moves, the diameter of the flip graph). Proving 8 is minimal needs an invariant (chains or cube counting) that the page only introduces in Problems 5-7. Remove this sentence here and either move it after Problem 7 as its own problem or leave it as an adult prompt.

edits.quote: For each number, draw the coverings you pass through (eight small hexagons, bottom half of page empty)
edits.fix: A 4-move loop and a 6-move loop pass through 4 + 6 = 10 coverings, but only 8 copies are printed. Add at least four more small hexagons in the empty lower half. (Answers: 4 and 6 are possible; 5 and 7 are impossible because the flip graph is bipartite.)

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 (page number set apart at the right margin)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

grades-4-5.summary: Rich and correct throughout. The 6 coverings of the small hexagon lead to the flip graph, then flip routes (8 and 4 moves), loop parity (4 and 6 yes, 5 and 7 no), chains (the example RLLR and the chains of A-D read correctly; 2 of the 4 requested chain pairs exist), how a move swaps an adjacent LR pair, and counting 20 coverings for both the one-chain board and the big hexagon. The edits are about sequencing: Problem 3 asks for a minimality proof before chains supply the tool, and Problem 4 is short of recording copies. There is more than forty minutes of work.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 sheet builds the up/down counting argument from concrete impossible boards through a proof, a generalization to any size, and an invent-your-own board, with every board at actual size and every answer correct.
overall.weakest: The K-1 sheet is a little short of forty minutes for a quick child and has small done-condition gaps (extra copies in Problem 4, no circle instruction in Problem 6), and the 4-5 sheet asks for a minimality proof in Problem 3 before introducing the chain tool.
